# The generated API, shape by shape

Every snippet below is the Kotlin the processor emits, taken from a generated file. Types are
written fully qualified in the output; they are shortened here only where the line would wrap.

## The file

```kotlin
// Generated by dev.modaal:mocks-processor. DO NOT EDIT.
// Regenerated at test compilation; generated output is never committed.
package dev.modaal.mocks.receipt

class ReceiptEnvironmentMock(
  staticConfig: ReceiptConfig,
) : ReceiptEnvironment {
```

The class is public, named `<Interface>Mock`, and declared in the interface's own package. Its
constructor carries one parameter per read-only requirement that has no guessable default, and
nothing else. Members are emitted name-sorted, whatever order the interface declares them in, and the
same interface always produces the same bytes.

## A method with one recordable parameter

```kotlin
override fun log(message: kotlin.String) {
  logCallCount += 1
  logArgs.add(message)
  logHandler?.invoke(message)
}
var logCallCount: kotlin.Int = 0
val logArgs: kotlin.collections.MutableList<kotlin.String> = mutableListOf()
var logHandler: ((kotlin.String) -> kotlin.Unit)? = null
```

The count and the argument are recorded **before** the handler runs, so a handler that throws does
not un-make the call.

## A method with several recordable parameters

Kotlin has no tuple, so the record is a nested data class named after the method:

```kotlin
data class MeasureArgs(
  val width: kotlin.Int,
  val height: kotlin.Int,
)
override fun measure(width: kotlin.Int, height: kotlin.Int, onDone: (kotlin.Int) -> kotlin.Unit): kotlin.Boolean {
  measureCallCount += 1
  measureArgs.add(MeasureArgs(width, height))
  measureHandler?.let { return it(width, height, onDone) }
  return false
}
val measureArgs: kotlin.collections.MutableList<MeasureArgs> = mutableListOf()
var measureHandler: ((kotlin.Int, kotlin.Int, (kotlin.Int) -> kotlin.Unit) -> kotlin.Boolean)? = null
```

A test asserts on it by value, through the nested class's qualified name:

```kotlin
assertEquals(listOf(ReceiptEnvironmentMock.MeasureArgs(width = 4, height = 3)), environment.measureArgs)
```

`onDone` is function-typed, so it reaches the handler and stays out of the record. A method whose
parameters are all function-typed, and a method with no parameters, get no `<fn>Args` member — assert
through the handler and the call count.

## A suspend method, and what an unset handler does

```kotlin
override suspend fun load(id: kotlin.String): ReceiptConfig {
  loadCallCount += 1
  loadArgs.add(id)
  loadHandler?.let { return it(id) }
  error("loadHandler expected to be set.")
}
var loadHandler: (suspend (kotlin.String) -> ReceiptConfig)? = null
```

`suspend` is carried into the handler's type. The fallback rules, in the order the generated code
applies them:

| the return type | what an unset handler returns |
| --- | --- |
| `Unit` | nothing; the handler is invoked if set and the method returns |
| `Flow<E>` | `<fn>Channel.receiveAsFlow()` |
| any nullable type | `null` |
| a type with a guessable default | that default |
| anything else | fails with `IllegalStateException` carrying `<fn>Handler expected to be set.` |

The guessable defaults:

| type | default |
| --- | --- |
| `Int`, `Long`, `Double`, `Float` | `0`, `0L`, `0.0`, `0.0f` |
| `Boolean` | `false` |
| `String` | `""` |
| `List`, `Map`, `Set` | `emptyList()`, `emptyMap()`, `emptySet()` |
| `MutableList`, `MutableMap`, `MutableSet` | `mutableListOf()`, `mutableMapOf()`, `mutableSetOf()` |

A nullable return therefore never fails an unseeded test: `findLabelHandler?.let { return it(id) }`
is followed by `return null`.

## A method returning `Flow`

The handler is read at call time and the counters wrap whichever stream the call produced:

```kotlin
override fun events(): kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow<ReceiptEvent> {
  eventsCallCount += 1
  return (eventsHandler?.invoke() ?: eventsChannel.receiveAsFlow())
    .onStart { eventsSubscribeCount += 1 }
    .onEach { value ->
      eventsOutputCount += 1
      eventsOutputs.add(value)
      eventsOutputHandler?.invoke(value)
    }
    .onCompletion { cause ->
      if (cause is kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException) eventsSubscribeCancelCount += 1
      else eventsCompletionCount += 1
    }
}
val eventsChannel: kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel<ReceiptEvent> =
  kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel(kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel.UNLIMITED)
```

The channel is unlimited, so a test may send before anyone collects, and `receiveAsFlow()` completes
when the channel closes and only then. Seeding `eventsHandler` takes precedence and needs no close;
its stream is counted the same way. Only an exact `Flow<E>` return gets a channel — a nullable
`Flow<E>?` falls back to `null`.

`<fn>SubscribeCount` counts collections; `<fn>OutputCount` and `<fn>Outputs` count and record each
delivered value and `<fn>OutputHandler` sees it after the record; `<fn>CompletionCount` counts the
stream ending or failing and `<fn>SubscribeCancelCount` a collection that stopped early. A value sent
while nobody collects counts nothing until it is delivered, and the counters are not synchronized —
collecting one member from two coroutines concurrently can lose an increment or a recorded value.

## Properties

Every property requirement carries the same members, and `_<prop>` is the value:

```kotlin
// var requirement: reads and writes are both counted. Construction counts neither.
override var volume: kotlin.Double
  get() {
    volumeGetCount += 1
    volumeGetHandler?.let { return it() }
    return _volume
  }
  set(value) {
    volumeSetCount += 1
    _volume = value
  }
var volumeGetCount: kotlin.Int = 0
var volumeGetHandler: (() -> kotlin.Double)? = null
var volumeSetCount: kotlin.Int = 0
var _volume: kotlin.Double = 0.0
```

A read-only requirement gets that getter, no setter, and an `override val`. Its store is seeded from
the guessable default, or from a constructor parameter of the declared name when the type has none:

```kotlin
override val idleTimeoutMs: kotlin.Long
  get() { … }                                      // the getter above, without the setter
var _idleTimeoutMs: kotlin.Long = 0L               // seeded from the guessable default
var _staticConfig: ReceiptConfig = staticConfig    // seeded from the constructor parameter
```

- `mock.<prop>` moves `<prop>GetCount`; `mock._<prop>` reads and writes the same value and moves no
  counter.
- `<prop>GetHandler` wins over the store on every read and never fails — the store always holds a
  value.
- `mock.<prop> = value` does not compile for a read-only requirement. Assign `mock._<prop>`.

A read-only `Flow` property is the one property with no store: `<prop>Channel` is its fallback, and
it carries the six stream members of §"A method returning `Flow`" as well. Its handler is read inside
the flow builder rather than in the getter, so one seeded after the code under test captured the flow
still decides the stream:

```kotlin
override val configUpdates: kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow<ReceiptConfig>
  get() {
    configUpdatesGetCount += 1
    return flow { emitAll(configUpdatesGetHandler?.invoke() ?: configUpdatesChannel.receiveAsFlow()) }
      .onStart { … }    // the same chain, on configUpdates
  }
var configUpdatesGetCount: kotlin.Int = 0
var configUpdatesGetHandler: (() -> kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow<ReceiptConfig>)? = null
val configUpdatesChannel: kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel<ReceiptConfig> = …
```

An interface of properties alone generates a constructor-seeded bag:

```kotlin
val dependency = ReceiptDependencyMock(config = config)   // `step: Double` defaulted to 0.0
```

Adding a member without a guessable default to such an interface breaks every construction of the
mock at compile time, which is the point of seeding through the constructor.

## Overloads

Overloads would collide on the shared bookkeeping names. The overload with the fewest parameters
keeps the plain name — so adding a wider overload later renames nothing an existing test uses — and
each other overload appends its capitalized parameter names:

```kotlin
fun update(id: String)                → updateCallCount, updateArgs, updateHandler
fun update(id: String, force: Boolean) → updateIdForceCallCount, updateIdForceArgs, updateIdForceHandler
```

## Inherited requirements

The mock implements the interface's full requirement set, inherited members included. A member with
an interface-default body keeps its default and gets no mock members.

## The same vocabulary in the Swift twin

A codebase that tests the same logic on both platforms gets one dialect. The Swift side is generated
by swift-sourcery-templates.

| Kotlin | Swift |
| --- | --- |
| `<fn>CallCount` | `<method>CallCount` |
| `<fn>Args` | `<method>Args` |
| `<fn>Handler` | `<method>Handler` |
| `<prop>GetCount`, `<prop>GetHandler`, on every property | `<var>GetCount`, `<var>GetHandler`, on every property |
| `<prop>SetCount` | `<var>SetCount` |
| `_<prop>` | `_<var>` |
| `<fn>Channel` for a `Flow` member, single-consumer | `<method>Subject` for an `AnyPublisher` member, broadcast to every subscriber |
| `<fn>SubscribeCount`, `<fn>SubscribeCancelCount`, `<fn>OutputCount`, `<fn>Outputs`, `<fn>OutputHandler`, `<fn>CompletionCount` | the same six on an `AnyPublisher` member |
| `<fn>Handler expected to be set.` | the same string |
| constructor-seeded bag | the initializer-seeded equivalent |
| no counterpart | `<method>EventCallCount`, `<method>EventHandler`, `<method>Events` for an `AnyObserver` member |
| no counterpart | `<method>CancelCallCount` / `<method>CancelHandler` for `AnyCancellable`, and the same pair for `Disposable` |
| no counterpart — targets are a build-script list | the per-declaration annotations `methodName`, `handler`, `init`, `const`, `subject`, `skipArgumentRecording` |

The names, the channel-backed stream shape and the failure string are shared deliberately. Renaming
one of them is a change to both generators, not a local refactor.
